title: Rashi's life
hook: a winemaker in Troyes who explained the Bible and Talmud

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbeinu Gershom, the light of the exile. Your line was don't read their letters. Today, a student of his students, in France.

A printed page of the Torah, the kind used for study. Look at the column beside the verses: small letters, a slightly different shape from the main text. Open a page of the Talmud, and there it is again, on the inner margin, close to the spine. The same voice on both, explaining a word here, a sentence there, answering the question a beginner was about to ask. That voice belongs to a man from a market town in Champagne, in France. He was a scholar. And tradition says he also worked with vines. Today, Rashi's life.
screen: `A COLUMN BESIDE THE VERSES.` → `THE SAME VOICE ON THE TALMUD.` → `A TOWN IN CHAMPAGNE.`

segments.voice: Rashi is a name from initials: Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, Solomon son of Isaac. He was from Troyes. As a young man he went to study in the Rhine towns, Mainz and Worms, with teachers who had learned from the circle of Rabbeinu Gershom. Then he came home and opened a school. Tradition says he made his living from vineyards, and readers point to how well his commentary knows pressing grapes and handling wine. Some historians ask whether that's a memory or a guess; the commentary itself is the evidence people bring. What he wrote is the point: the plain meaning of the Torah and the Talmud, word by word, for anyone sitting down to learn. Take the first verse. In the JPS translation: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." Rashi's first comment asks a student's question. If the Torah is a book of commandments, why doesn't it start with the first commandment given to Israel as a people, in Exodus? Why start with creation? He answers with a teaching of the rabbis: the story of the world comes first, because the whole earth belongs to God, who gives each land to whom God chooses. Notice the habits. He uses the French of his town, written in Hebrew letters, to explain hard words. He says when he doesn't know. And he writes briefly. His commentary is still printed beside the text: a man who, tradition says, lived by his town's ordinary trade, and made the hardest books readable.
screen: `RABBI SHLOMO YITZCHAKI, OF TROYES.` · `TRADITION SAYS: HE TENDED VINES.` · then, large: `IN THE BEGINNING GOD CREATED.` · `PLAIN WORDS, FRENCH WORDS, I DON'T KNOW.`

segments.voice: Think of the work your days are full of, a shift, a commute, a desk, and find one small seam where learning could live: ten minutes before work, a verse on a card in your pocket. Picture it turning over quietly while you work, the way a grape slowly becomes wine. If you pray, you can ask in your own words for both.
Rashi's life. Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki of Troyes: by tradition a vintner, and the teacher whose commentary sits beside the Torah and the Talmud. Today's word.
Your line: vintner and teacher. Ordinary work, with learning right beside it. That's day nine hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Jews studying the weekly Torah portion often read it with Rashi's commentary, and his notes appear on the inner margin of the printed Talmud page.

chat.says: Why is Rashi's commentary printed on almost every study page of the Torah?
options: He explained the plain meaning word by word, for anyone sitting down to learn.
He wrote for advanced scholars, so it covers the hardest mystical ideas.
He headed the Rhine academies, so his notes became the official ones.
chat.meaning: Rashi explained hard words, said when he didn't know, and wrote briefly, so beginners could read the Torah and Talmud.
